Posted November 10, 2000
Special to MarijuanaNews.com

In Massachusetts: Money Misses, Grassroots Gain!
November 9, 2000
By Michael D. Cutler, Esq.(MarijuanaNews note: My good friend Mike Cutler is a Massachusetts attorney and long time supporter of NORML and drug war opponent. He is a patient advocate for the mentally ill in Massachusetts.)
See
Ralph Seeley, Freedom Fighter -- Obituary by Michael D. Cutler, Esq
and
NIDA’s Traveling Road Show " Understanding Drug Abuse " By Michael D. Cutler, Esq

If there were competent journalists, we wouldn’t have Prohibition (which regular MarijuanaNews readers recognize as Cowan-speak), but an ordinary journalist (and no media outlet pays me; my day job is mental health lawyering) might have compared the national results of drug reform ballot initiatives and written this headline:
" Outside Drug Reform Funders Carry California, Colorado, Nevada, Lose Massachusetts. "

There is another story, however, buried beneath the bad news, and it will keep reform hopes alive. The bad news: a 47-53% defeat of a Massachusetts state-wide initiate, which if adopted would have changed existing law to divert first and second offense drug offenders,
including small dealers, from mandatory imprisonment to treatment, funded by the diversion of civil asset property forfeitures from prosecutors and the police to a fund dedicated to treatment services. But as Paul Harvey might say, " Now for the rest of the story " –

In four voting districts throughout Massachusetts, local referenda to endorse new laws that would fine instead of jail adult recreational pot users, and permit medical marijuana use, passed by Yes vs. No margins ranging from 61% to 67.5%!

The MA ballot initiatives this year included both state-wide questions, and several local district questions. State-wide Question 8, advertised as " drug money for drug treatment, " received nearly one million dollars from " out-of-state " funders.

In four MA state legislative districts, however, unfunded reformers associated with the state NORML affiliate (the Massachusetts Cannabis Reform Coalition, " MassCann NORML " ) collected signatures to put on selected local ballots, then campaigned for, Question 9.

In three jurisdictions, Question 9 instructed the local representative or senator to support legislation to decriminalize (fine instead of imprisoning) adult marijuana possession; the other voting district, on Cape Cod, endorsed legal use of marijuana for medical purposes.

While the highly funded campaign, which was endorsed by three former state Attorney Generals and a sitting Congressman, did not succeed; a rag-tag army (less than ten) of 20-somethings and 50-somethings snatched victory for drug policy reform, from the jaws of better funded defeat.

In Medford, Somerville, Winchester and Woburn, out of 50,000 voters, 33,000 said yes to ending the jailing of adult marijuana users; excluding blanks, the Yes beat the No, 66-34%. In Framingham, from 17,000 total voters, nearly 10,000 said yes; excluding blanks, Yes carried 67.5% over Prohibition supporters.

From 23,000 voters in Ipswich (fried clam heaven) and northeastern Essex County, 50.1% voted Yes, and reform outvoted Prohibition (excluding blanks) 62-38%. On Cape Cod, from 25,000 voters, 52% voted to legalize medical marijuana, outvoting believers in patient suffering by 61-39%.

Lessons for future reform abound, and could support many articles of varying perspectives:

  • how much money is enough to fund a reform message that will resonate effectively and penetrate enough households to swing the uncertain? (Tracking polls show that on Question 8, nearly 100% of the undecided voters ended up voting No.)

  • how to better counter the scare tactics of law enforcement opponents.

  • how to activate natural allies like social workers and other treatment providers, students, mental and public health professionals in academia, government and private contract providers.

  • how to break up or break through the media hegemony with prosecutors, who are vital news resources for journalists (did someone mention incompetent journalism, again?).


Permit me a few, narrower observations.

On the positive side of outside funding, access to serious money has attracted to drug policy a group of opinion leaders (media consultant former journalists, lobbyists, mental and public health professionals and academics) who ordinarily speak only to other opinion leaders, and rarely with ordinary people. Being for the most part intelligent, competent and successful in reaching the highest level of hired gunmanship for commercial ballot initiatives, these wise-guys (actually, mostly gals in MA) who had accepted Prohibition as the only way, required little exposure to the logic of reform to genuinely " get it. "

This issue appears to have become more than a job for many of them, who I hope will become more active and very valuable allies in convincing legislators that voting for reform will not convert them into a former legislators.

On the downside, the funded results compared to the volunteer results demonstrate the critical value of grassroots organizing.

Public safety and Prohibitionist propaganda live closer to the hearts than the heads of voters. Media-buys alone, without follow up from trusted friends or respected professionals, will not persuade the uneducated or over-programmed. When in doubt, they vote to maintain the status quo. Grassroots organizing means the reform message comes to voters not only from the impersonal tube or radio, but more persuasively from their neighborhood, from a local church, from a local leaflet distributor whose children go to the same school as your son or daughter.

Question 8 voters were uncertain about whether treating hard drug users caused them greater risk than incarceration; Question 9 voters were far more certain that they had far less to fear from freeing marijuana smokers. Not only the message counts; the messenger counts, too. We will never know whether more money for greater market penetration would have saved Question 8, although I’m told that of all the outside funded television advertisements nationally, the best were produced in and for Massachusetts. Also in this same election, five-million dollars of HMO funding convinced a similar 47-53% split of voters to defeat universal health care.

We do know, however, that we have a message that voters are ready to hear. That light at the end of the tunnel certainly needs money to burn brighter, but it also needs more people carrying torches
